analysis.one_liner: Requires online platforms to safeguard minors from harmful design features and bans targeted ads to children and teens.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the Senate 91-3 with near-unanimous bipartisan support, but the House never voted on the final version before the Congress ended, so it became law for no one.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill started as a small government-housekeeping measure requiring agencies to list outdated reports they no longer need. Along the way, Congress used it as the vehicle for a much larger package: the Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act, which would require social media, gaming, and streaming platforms to protect minors from addictive design features, bullying, sexual exploitation, and ads for drugs, tobacco, gambling, and alcohol. It would also update children's online privacy law to cover teens under 17 and ban targeted advertising aimed at kids and teens. The Senate passed it twice, the House passed it once by voice vote, and the Senate approved the final version 91-3 — but the House never voted on that final version, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers who use social media, gaming, and video platforms, and their parents, who would get default privacy and safety settings, tools to limit screen time and purchases, a ban on targeted advertising to minors, and new independent research on social media harms.

how_it_helps.text: Platforms must use reasonable care to prevent and mitigate harms to minors including anxiety, depression, eating disorders, substance use, addiction-like usage patterns, bullying, sexual exploitation, and marketing of drugs, tobacco, gambling, and alcohol.

Platforms must give minors default-on safeguards: limits on who can contact them, controls over addictive design features like infinite scrolling and autoplay, opt-outs of personalized recommendation systems, and location-sharing restrictions, plus parental tools for younger children.
The bill bans collecting or using children's and teens' personal information for individual-specific advertising, extending child privacy law to teens under 17 for the first time.

Large platforms must publish annual, independently audited public reports on risks of harm to minors, and federal agencies must commission at least five comprehensive studies on social media's effects on minors.

It also carries the original purpose: agencies must list outdated or duplicative congressionally required reports in their budget justifications and recommend ending, modifying, or consolidating them.
It lets users switch off algorithmic feeds that use their inferred data, requiring platforms to offer a chronological, non-profiled content option.

analysis.who_pays: Large social media, online gaming, video streaming, and digital advertising companies, which would have to redesign features, run third-party audits, publish annual transparency reports, and lose targeted-advertising revenue from minors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large social media, gaming, and ad-tech firms

drawbacks.text: Platforms would have to determine which users are minors using actual knowledge or 'knowledge fairly implied on the basis of objective circumstances,' which could push services toward broader age estimation of all users, raising privacy and free-expression concerns even though the bill forbids requiring new age-gating.

The duty-of-care requirement could lead platforms to restrict or restrict-by-default content that minors can access — such as health or identity-related material — to avoid legal risk, a trade-off critics of online safety bills have raised.

The definitions are broad — covering any platform 'reasonably likely to be used by a minor,' including online games with chat — so compliance costs would fall heavily on smaller companies as well as large ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real but narrow: stronger safety defaults, privacy protections, and transparency for minors in exchange for compliance burdens and less targeted advertising revenue for tech companies, and some risk that platforms over-restrict teen access to content to limit liability. On balance the package is a consumer-protection measure aimed squarely at some of the largest and most profitable companies in the economy.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the final version 91-3, but House leaders never brought that version up for a vote before the Congress ended, so the bill died.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced as the Eliminate Useless Reports Act, requiring agencies to list outdated or duplicative reporting requirements in budget justifications.
The Senate Homeland Security Committee reported it favorably in August 2023, and the Senate passed it by unanimous consent in December 2023.

In May 2024, the House passed an amended version by voice vote under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure used for noncontroversial bills — that turned the bill into the Kids Online Safety and Privacy Act.
The Senate invoked cloture on the House-amended bill 86-1, meaning 86 senators voted to allow a final vote, with 45 Democrats, 38 Republicans, and 3 independents in favor.
On July 30, 2024, the Senate concurred in the House amendment with its own amendment by a 91-3 vote, with 43 Democrats, 44 Republicans, and 4 independents in favor.
The final Senate-amended version was sent to the House on July 31, 2024, but the House never voted on it, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Social media, gaming, and digital advertising companies are better off: the bill that would have restricted their design features and targeted advertising to minors died without a House vote, despite overwhelming Senate support.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan at every recorded step: cloture passed 86-1 (45 D, 38 R, 3 I in favor) and final Senate passage passed 91-3 (43 D, 44 R, 4 I in favor), with no partisan divide. The bill's death was not a party-line vote — it simply never came up in the House.

industries.note: The bill would force large platforms to build default-on safety controls for minors, restrict addictive design features like infinite scrolling, and publish independently audited annual reports on harms to minors, creating legal exposure under FTC and state-enforcement provisions. These costs are the direct source of the bill's benefits for kids and parents.

The privacy title bans collecting or using children's and teens' personal information for individual-specific advertising and extends child privacy rules to teens under 17, cutting off a lucrative segment of targeted advertising. Parents and teens would see less profiling in exchange.

Online games with chat, microtransactions, or user uploads count as covered platforms, so they would owe the same safeguards for minors, restrictions on design features, and parental purchase controls.

The bill covers streaming services but gives a lighter-touch compliance path if their content is preselected rather than user-generated, so large streamers face fewer obligations than social networks.
